q: Roussillon may blend a second, coarser Muscat into its fortified sweet wines, while the Rhone version admits a single Muscat and no other. Which variety?
exp: The small-berried white Muscat is the perfumed one, orange blossom and crushed grape, and it is all the Rhone appellation will take, its red-berried form counting as the same variety. Rivesaltes and its neighbours lean on Muscat of Alexandria as well, which is fatter and less floral. Muscat Ottonel is a nineteenth-century crossing grown in Alsace and central Europe, and Muscat Hamburg is a table grape.

q: Which variety is prized in southern rose for perfume and freshness rather than for power?
exp: It gives pale colour, floral aroma and low tannin, so it dilutes weight in the best sense. In red blends it is the grape that keeps a hot vintage drinkable.

q: Bottles from the valley climb through a hierarchy of appellations. Which sequence runs from the broadest tier to the narrowest?
opts: Cotes du Rhone, then Villages, then Villages with a named commune, then the crus
Villages, then Cotes du Rhone, then the crus, then Villages with a named commune
Cotes du Rhone, then the crus, then Villages, then Villages with a named commune
The crus, then Cotes du Rhone, then Villages, then Villages with a named commune
exp: Each step up tightens yields and narrows the ground. A cru drops the Cotes du Rhone name entirely and stands on its own, which is the clearest signal on the label.

q: Adding a commune name such as Sablet or Seguret after Cotes du Rhone Villages signals what?
opts: The wine comes from a single estate
The commune has been promoted to cru status
The wine may be sold only within France
A smaller area with stricter rules
exp: The ground is tighter and the yields lower than for plain Villages. The named communes are the waiting room for promotion, several current crus passed through it, and they are reliably the best value in the valley.

q: May a grower in the northern half of the valley label a wine Cotes du Rhone?
opts: Yes, it covers the whole valley
Only in years when no cru wine is declared
Only if the wine is white
No, it applies to the southern half only
exp: The regional appellation runs from Vienne to Avignon, though the overwhelming majority of the wine is southern. A northern grower with young vines or declassified fruit uses it regularly.

q: Which trio of grapes forms the backbone of most red Cotes du Rhone?
exp: Grenache brings the sweet fruit and alcohol, Syrah the colour and pepper, Mourvedre the tannin and savour. The abbreviation has followed the blend around the world.

q: A cold, dry wind funnels down the valley from the north, sometimes for days on end. What is it called?
exp: It accelerates as the valley narrows and can blow at over a hundred kilometres an hour. Locals blame it for a great deal more than viticulture.

q: Growers put up with that wind for one clear benefit. What is it?
opts: It raises humidity around the bunches
It ripens the grapes by warming the vineyard
It dries the vines and holds fungal disease in check
It carries mineral dust onto the leaves
exp: A dry canopy is why organic farming is so much easier here than in a damp maritime region. The cost is broken shoots and vines under stress in a hard spring.

q: Low bush-trained vines carrying neither wire nor stake are the classic southern answer to that wind. What is that training called?
exp: The short trunk keeps the vine stable and its own canopy shades the fruit from fierce sun. Newer plantings are often trellised instead, so that machines can work the rows.

q: Thin, free-draining rock on the steep northern slopes against deep beds of stone on the southern plain. Which pairing names the two?
opts: Chalk in the north and clay in the south
Granite in the north and galets roules in the south
Volcanic basalt in the north and limestone in the south
Sand in the north and slate in the south
exp: Granite gives the taut, mineral frame of northern Syrah; the stones of the south store heat and push Grenache toward ripeness and alcohol. The contrast explains most of the difference in the glass.

q: A beverage is made by converting rice starch into sugar and fermenting it, with no still involved at any point. Which drink is that?
exp: Sake is brewed, closer in method to beer than to wine, and never distilled. The other three are spirits, which is why they arrive at far higher strengths.

q: Grains chosen for brewing carry a chalky opaque centre that table rice lacks. What is that core called?
exp: The shinpaku is loose starch that the mould can penetrate easily. Brewing varieties also grow larger grains with less protein and fat in the outer layers.

q: Which named rice variety is the most sought after by brewers, grown chiefly in Hyogo prefecture?
exp: Yamada Nishiki is treated as the benchmark and commands a premium at competition level. Gohyakumangoku belongs to Niigata and Omachi to Okayama; Koshihikari is an eating rice.

q: Roughly four fifths of what ends up in the bottle is a single ingredient. Which one?
exp: Because water dominates the volume, its mineral profile shapes the finished style, and breweries have historically been sited on a particular spring or well.

q: Brewing water rich in minerals such as potassium and magnesium pushes the ferment which way?
opts: Faster and more vigorous, giving a firmer, drier sake
It stops fermentation before the yeast finishes
Slower and cooler, giving a sweeter, rounder sake
It has no measurable effect on fermentation
exp: Nada in Hyogo built its name on hard water known as miyamizu. Kyoto's Fushimi district sits on soft water and is known for a gentler, softer style.

q: A label states a seimaibuai of 50 percent. What does that figure tell you?
opts: Half the finished sake is water
The sake rested for half a year before release
Half of each grain has been milled away
Half the rice used was ordinary table rice
exp: The ratio names what remains, not what was removed, which is the commonest misreading. The lower the number, the more of the grain has gone to dust.
